topics.title: Reddit's lawsuit against Anthropic just cleared its first legal hurdle
topics.why: A UK court sided with an AI firm over a photo agency while a California judge let most of Reddit's scraping claims against Anthropic survive demurrer this fall, and a $3.1B music-publisher suit and the Authors Guild case are still pending -- training-data copyright exposure is turning from a theoretical risk into a real line item.

topics.title: The November jobs report is the first real test of the AI-layoffs story
topics.why: Challenger's next monthly layoff count lands in early November right as AI-attributed cuts have been climbing all year, even though a widely-cited NBER survey found 90% of executives see zero employment impact from AI at their own companies -- the gap between the headline and the internal data is the story.

topics.title: The $61k-to-$136k job nobody puts on a resume: training the models
topics.why: Outlier, Mercor, Scale AI, and DataAnnotation are quietly absorbing a wave of contract hiring as foundation labs chase evaluation data, and the reported pay spread between 'labeler' and 'reviewer' work is wide enough to plan an actual pivot around.

topics.title: Companies say they'd rather see your AI skills than your diploma
topics.why: A fresh round of 2026 hiring commentary and UK wage data point the same direction: demonstrated AI proficiency is outweighing degrees in screening and carrying a real wage premium, a shift worth acting on before it's priced into every job posting.

topics.title: AI didn't just automate gig work -- it started deciding who gets it
topics.why: As AI-driven matching spreads from ride-hailing into freelance and knowledge work, workers describe opaque ranking systems acting like an invisible manager -- the same platforms carry both the opportunity and the risk, which is the more honest framing than either hype or doom.
